title: Regional egress rate caps and graceful shedder for dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Dedicated fleets serving enterprise workloads sometimes experience cross-tenant spikes that saturate regional egress (bandwidth and token throughput) and reduce SLO compliance for latency-sensitive customers. Existing admission controls are fleet-global and reactive; they do not enforce region-aware caps or provide graceful degradation for high-priority routes. This ticket proposes a regionally aware egress rate capping layer and a graceful shedder that preserves headroom for critical traffic while shedding best-effort requests in a controlled way.
technical_design: Goal: implement a lightweight admission control module (regional-egress-admitter) that runs as a sidecar or in the front proxy for Dedicated pools. Key components: 1) Regional token buckets: maintain per-region and per-fleet token buckets. Tokens represent allowed token-output (tokenized model tokens) and request-equivalence units (REQUs) so we can cap both bandwidth and expensive long-sequence requests. 2) Priority-aware soft queues: incoming requests are classified by route priority (reserved, standard, best-effort). Reserved requests can borrow a small configurable headroom from region pool; best-effort requests enqueue into per-priority queues with soft timeouts. 3) Graceful shedding policy: when the regional bucket is below threshold, signal a soft-shed mode — stop admitting best-effort, start rejecting with 429 + Retry-After and a machine-readable body explaining reason and fallback suggestions. We expose two shedding levels: soft (queue freeze + reject lowest-priority) and hard (reject all non-reserved). 4) Concurrency fencing and fairness: limit concurrent in-flight requests per-tenant to avoid noisy neighbors; use token accounting that charges multi-turn chats against the same tenant bucket to prevent abuse. 5) Autoscaler tie-in: admission signals (headroom_used_pct, sustained_reject_rate) are emitted as metrics and consumed by the Dedicated autoscaler to trigger scale-up proactively rather than waiting for tail latency SLO breaches. 6) Backpressure to clients: for streaming endpoints, when headroom is low we prefer to accept but limit chunk rate (throttled streaming) and notify clients. 7) Open config and runtime knobs: caps per-region, per-fleet, per-tenant, per-route; queue sizes; per-priority timeouts; and sampling rates for telemetry. Implementation notes: - Use a leaky-bucket variant with moving-window smoothing to account for burstable traffic and avoid oscillation. - Store per-tenant and per-region counters in an in-memory sharded map with eviction for stale tenants. - Admission controller API: Admit(request_meta) -> { admit: bool, mode: "accept|queue|reject|throttle", retry_after_sec?: int, reason?: string, trace_id?: string } - Reject codes: 429 (rate limit), 503 (temporary unavailable when hard-shed), with structured JSON response and a small set of hints for SDKs (fallback model, reduce max_tokens, backoff seconds). - Metrics emitted: region_bucket_tokens, tenant_bucket_tokens, admit_rate_by_priority, queue_depth_by_priority, reject_rate_by_reason, headroom_pct, latency_p99_by_priority. - Tracing: attach admit decision trace_id to requests for debugging and correlation with Console dashboards.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature gate behind runtime flag and config for a single non-production region. 2) Smoke test with synthetic traffic generator that exercises long sequences and bursty patterns. 3) Observe metrics and ensure no increase in p50/p95 for reserved routes. 4) Canary: enable for a small set of customers in a single region with monitoring alerts (reject_rate > 0.5% triggers rollback). 5) Incremental region rollout over two weeks while keeping autoscaler thresholds conservative. 6) Post-rollout: 30-day monitoring window, tune bucket sizes and queue timeouts based on real traffic. 7) Documentation: update Dedicated docs and SDK error handling section with new error codes and suggested client backoff behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Regional token buckets enforce configured throughput caps per region and per-fleet and do not allow sustained token output over cap.
Priority-aware admission differentiates reserved, standard, and best-effort routes and preserves headroom for reserved traffic under spike conditions.
Reject responses include structured JSON with code, hint, and trace_id; SDKs can parse Retry-After and fallback suggestions.
Telemetry exposes metrics listed in the design and integrates with Console dashboards and alerting rules.
Autoscaler consumes admission metrics and initiates scale-up within configured thresholds in a controlled manner during synthetic load tests.
End-to-end tests and chaos scenarios (node loss, sudden 10x traffic) demonstrate graceful degradation rather than SLO-wide outage for reserved tenants.
Feature gate and rollout succeeded in canary region with no manual rollback and reject_rate <= 1% for reserved routes over 48h.
All new code has unit tests and integration tests; PRs reviewed by runtime and capacity owners.
notes: Trade-offs considered: strictly enforcing hard caps reduces customer surprise but can increase request churn; we prefer soft shedding with explicit client hints where possible.

Interaction with KV cache: long-lived cached prefixes reduce token emission; admission accounting should charge on emitted tokens, not input length. Ensure accurate token accounting for cached responses.
Edge-case: burst from many small tenants can still exhaust region capacity; consider a tenant fair-share scheduler as a follow-up (possible sub-issue).
This ticket intentionally separates regional egress (tokens) from CPU/GPU scheduling; we rely on autoscaler for node provisioning based on admission signals.
